note: The library belongs to W1-17 and to RI-LOR03; these six exist because RI-UIX05's `ui-book` fixture needs 'three books spanning the length distribution' and because a reading screen with nothing in it cannot be measured. They are written to be read, they carry prose directions (RI-WLD06 L3) rather than coordinates, and two of them disagree with each other on a named fact and are not reconciled anywhere (RI-LOR03: no book is corrected).

books.title: Instruction, with the compass
books.author: unsigned; the box-maker's hand
books.text:
Open the lid flat. Let the needle stop before you read it; it will swing twice and then a third time, smaller, and the third swing is the true one.

The needle finds north. It does not find your road, your house, your ship or the person you are looking for. If you wanted a thing that found those, you have bought the wrong object and no one will refund you.

Do not carry it open. Do not carry it near the iron of a blade. Do not leave it in the sun, and do not, whatever a Legion factor tells you, believe that a second needle laid beside the first improves it.

books.title: Crate tally, three counts
books.author: three hands, unsigned
books.text:
First count, in a clerk's hand: eleven crates landed, eleven crates stored, seal intact on nine.

Second count, in a heavier hand, in the margin: nine crates. Nine. Counted them myself, twice, and I want that written where it can be seen.

Third count, in pencil, in a hand that has been taught to write and not much more: eleven. But two of them is empty and light as nothing and I lifted them both.

Under all three, in the first hand again, and pressed hard enough to score the paper: The count is eleven. Do not write on this page again.

books.title: Ledger leaf, water-damaged
books.author: Provincial Office of Argonia
books.text:
PROVINCIAL OFFICE OF ARGONIA — REGISTER OF PERSONS, PART SEVEN

The left column is names and it has survived. Eleven of them. Deek-Ei. Waneela. Marsh-of-Nine. Teeus-Ahai. Sees-the-Weir. Hlaalu Verim, who is not Saxhleel and is in this register anyway. Ashaam. Nine-Toes. Reeh. Ulen Dral. And one that the water took the first half of, so that all that is left of a person's name on the page is the word ma.

The second column is where they were recorded and it has mostly survived. Lilmoth, Lilmoth, Lilmoth, Stormhold, Lilmoth, Gideon, Lilmoth, Blackrose, Lilmoth, Gideon, Lilmoth.

The third column is what was done and it has not survived at all. There is one word visible at the very bottom of the leaf, below the last name, in the hand of whoever closed the page: sufficient.

books.title: A letter, sealed
books.author: a clerk of the Provincial Office
books.text:
To Serjo Dral, at the third house past the tannery in Stormhold, and to him only.

The matter you raised at the spring assize has been considered and is closed. It is closed for the reason you were given and not for the reason you believe, and you will not raise it again.

You asked what the Office intends to do about the count. The Office intends to record the count. That is the whole of what an office does and you have been in the province long enough to know it.

The bearer of this letter is not in your employ, is not in ours, and has not been told what this says. Do not ask them. Do not keep them. Pay them what was agreed at Lilmoth and let them go, and if you cannot manage that, understand that the next letter will not come by hand.

Burn this.

books.title: The Topal Shore Run, as it is Actually Sailed
books.author: Sees-the-Weir, pilot, and a second hand arguing
books.text:
This is not a chart. A chart is a picture of a coast drawn by somebody who has never had to leave it in the dark, and it will kill you. This is the order you meet things in, which is the only order that matters when you are on the water and the light has gone.

Out of Lilmoth you keep the fish-drying racks on your right until the smell stops. That is not a joke and it is not approximate; the racks run a full half-mile and the wind off them is the only landmark you get in the first hour. When you can no longer smell them you have cleared the shoal.

Then you look for the three dead trees. There were four. The second hand has written here: there are two. I have counted them from the water more times than I care to say in the last year and there are two. Sees-the-Weir has written under that: there are three, and one of them is lying down, and if you cannot recognise a dead tree lying down you should not be piloting.

After the trees the shore turns and you lose it. Do not follow it. The bay it turns into has a mouth and a false mouth and they look identical from a boat at any hour. Instead, hold the heading you had when you passed the trees, count a slow four hundred, and the Border Falls come up on your left ear before they come up on your eye. You will hear them a long time before you see them. When you hear them you are past the false mouth.

From the falls, the black water is on your left the whole way to the ford. Keep it there. Everything that has gone wrong on this run in living memory has gone wrong because somebody put the black water on their right for what they thought was a shortcut across the bar.

At the ford, do not cross at the ford. The name is old and it is a lie. There has not been a crossing there since the drowning and the bottom is fouled with what is left of it. Go up two bends. There is a xanmeer on the north side with its top out of the water and its stair going down into it, and the crossing is level with the third step from the water, and it is safe if the third step is dry and it is not safe if it is not. That is the whole test. Do not improve on it.

Second hand: it is the fourth step.

Sees-the-Weir: it is the third step and I have been doing this since before you could swim.

Second hand: I have measured it.

Past the crossing you are on the Blackrose reach and anyone can pilot the Blackrose reach. Wake me.

One more thing, and it is the thing the Office will not print. If you are carrying for a factor and he tells you to run the outside of the bar at night to save a tide, he is not saving a tide. He is moving something he does not want counted at Lilmoth, and the run he is asking you for is the run that drowned the two boats in the wet season before last. Ask him to write the instruction down. He will not. That is your answer and you may take it as far as you like.

books.title: What the Water Took: an Account of the Wet Season of the Thirty-Ninth Year
books.author: Waneela of Lilmoth, who was there
books.text:
I am writing this because a man in Gideon has printed a book about a thing I saw, and he was not there, and he was not born.

His book says we drowned them by sorcery. I want to set down what we actually did, in the order we did it, so that somebody in fifty years has the choice of two accounts instead of one.

The dry month came early that year and it came hard. The reach above the ford went down to a walk. You could see the bottom of it, which nobody alive had seen, and there were things on the bottom that people came from three settlements to look at and then stopped talking about. The weirs upriver were standing in air. My great-grandmother's weir, the big one at the second bend, had been in water since her mother's time and that year it was in nothing at all, and she went up and stood in the frame of it for most of an afternoon.

The Dunmer column came down out of the Salt Hills in the second week of that month, which they thought was clever. In a wet year they could not have come that way at all. They had two hundred and some, and slave-takers with them, and they meant to cross at the ford because the ford was the only place a column with carts could cross, and they knew that because everybody knows that, and they had been told it was passable because it was.

Here is what my great-grandmother did. She opened the weirs.

That is all she did. There were four of them above the ford and she and her brothers walked up the dry reach and lifted the gates on all four, which is a morning's work for people who know the gates, and then they walked back down and sat on the bank at Lilmoth and waited two days.

What is behind a fish-weir in this country is not a pond. It is a season. Every weir on that reach had been holding back the whole of the wet before, because that is what a weir is for, and the marsh above them was full and had been full for a year, and none of it had anywhere to go while the gates were shut. When the gates came up it did not come down as a wave. That is what the Gideon man got wrong, along with everything else. It came down as a rise. It took most of a day. The column was in the ford, and in the shallows on both sides of the ford, and strung back up the road for half a mile with the carts, and the water came up around them at the speed of a man walking, and it did not stop coming up until it was dark.

They had all that time. That is the part nobody writes down. They had the whole day. A man could have walked out of it at any point in the first six hours and most of them did. Most of them lived. What they lost was the carts, and the carts had the food and the ropes and the chains, and a slaving column that has lost its chains in a marsh in the wet is not a column any more, it is four hundred people who need to get back up a pass before dark.

Afterwards the Dunmer said sorcery, and I understand why. It is easier to be beaten by a wizard than by a woman who understood water. And there is a second reason, which is that if it was sorcery then it was a crime, and if it was a woman opening four gates on her own weirs on her own reach then it was not a crime at all, and they had nothing to take to the Provincial Office.

They took it anyway. The Office recorded it. That is the whole of what an office does.

My great-grandmother was asked, at the assize, whether she had known the column was coming. She said yes. She was asked whether she had opened the gates because of it. She said yes. She was asked whether she had intended the column to drown. She said: I intended the water to go where water goes.

They could not do anything with that and they let her go, and she went home and shut the gates again, because the reach needed to fill, and it was a poor fish year for three years after and everybody blamed her for that too.

One thing more, for whoever reads this. There is a book by Hlaalu-Teeth of Gideon called On the Drowning at the Ford, and it says my great-grandmother worked a spell over the water. It also says the crossing is safe at the third step of the xanmeer stair. I have written to him twice about the first thing and he has not answered, and I have not written to him about the second, because if he wants to test it he may.
